newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Diana meets Bosnian boys wounded by landmines.
newsitem.headline: Diana meets Bosnian boys wounded by landmines.

text.p: Britain's Princess Diana met two boys from opposite sides of Bosnia's ethnic divide on Saturday to hear how they lost their legs in landmine accidents.
Diana, visiting Bosnia as part of her international crusade against mines, spoke with a Serb and a Moslem boy who were wounded by mine blasts on different sides of the former front line.
"I went to the woods to play and when I was playing I found an anti-tank mine. I started playing with it and it exploded," Zdravko Beric, 12, a Serb, told reporters before meeting Diana.

The fair-haired boy was driven across the boundary separating Serb-controlled and Moslem-Croat territory to meet the princess, whose visit was aimed at highlighting the plight of victims injured by mines left behind by war.

In the village of Klokotnica outside the central town of Zenica, Diana also spoke to 14-year-old Malik Bradoric, a Moslem, who was injured by a landmine as he was helping his father collect food near an old battlefield.

The two boys giggled and walked arm-in-arm as they waited for Diana to arrive, apparently immune to the nationalist hatreds that helped fuel the 1992-95 war between the Moslem-led central government and Serb separatists.
Diana, dressed casually in a white shirt and denim jeans, visited the Moslem boy's family in their simple brick house and tried cake prepared by Malik.
Unable to communicate except through interpreters, the princess tried to convey her sympathy by embracing the boys and their relatives.
Nevresa Bradoric, mother of Malik, said she had never heard of Diana and thought some sort of general would be paying her family a visit.
Like other Bosnians, she seemed puzzled by the calvacade of buses, cars, press and police following the princess and the photographers lined up two-deep beside her vegetable garden.

Diana's trip came as speculation about her love life hit new heights. London tabloids splashed photos of her with film producer Dodi Fayed, son of Egyptian tycoon Mohammed Al-Fayed, who owns London's luxury department store Harrods.
Her marriage to British royal heir Prince Charles ended in divorce in 1996 after 15 years.

The 36-year-old princess was invited by the Washington-based Landmine Survivors Network to raise awareness of the terrible toll caused by mines in a three-day visit to Bosnia's Moslem-Croat Federation.

Diana held several other emotionally-charged meetings with mine victims on Friday and Saturday, listening to the problems they face trying to obtain proper prosthetics and rehabilitation in a country devastated by war.
She was due to attend a "sitting" volleyball match between mine victims in Zenica later on Saturday.
Ken Rutherford, the American co-founder of the network who lost both his legs in Somalia in 1993, said Diana would make a "huge difference" to the cause.

At a dinner meeting on Friday with a group of 20 mine victims, Diana had taken copious notes throughout the meal, he said. "She's not faking. I'm a landmine victim myself and I know when people are faking."

Diana was not expected to visit Serb-controlled territory in Bosnia due to security concerns following a raid by British special forces last month to arrest two Serbs wanted by the United Nations war crimes tribunal.
One of the suspects was shot dead while resisting arrest, while the other was apprehended and sent to The Hague for trial.
